description: Comprehensive Physics question bank based on FDA & SDA competitive examination study material. Covers Mechanics; Properties of Matter and Fluids; Heat and Thermodynamics; Electricity; Magnetism and Electromagnetism; Light and Optics; Sound and Waves; Modern Physics.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a physical quantity?

options.A: A property that can be measured and expressed by a numerical value and a unit
options.B: A property that cannot be measured
options.C: A quantity that has only direction
options.D: A quantity that has only magnitude

questions.explanation: A physical quantity is a property that can be measured and expressed by a numerical value and a unit; examples: length, mass, time and temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are fundamental (base) quantities?

options.A: Quantities obtained by combining base quantities
options.B: Independent physical quantities not defined in terms of other physical quantities

questions.explanation: Fundamental (base) quantities are independent physical quantities not defined in terms of other physical quantities. The seven SI base quantities are length, mass, time, electric current, thermodynamic temperature, amount of substance and luminous intensity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is the SI base unit of length?

options.A: Centimetre (cm)
options.B: Metre (m)

questions.explanation: The SI base unit of length is the metre (m).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI base unit of mass?

options.A: Gram (g)
options.B: Pound (lb)

questions.explanation: The SI base unit of mass is the kilogram (kg).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI base unit of time?

options.A: Minute (min)
options.B: Hour (h)

questions.explanation: The SI base unit of time is the second (s).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI base unit of electric current?

options.A: Volt (V)
options.B: Ampere (A)

questions.explanation: The SI base unit of electric current is the ampere (A).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature?

options.A: Celsius (°C)
options.B: Fahrenheit (°F)

questions.explanation: The SI base unit of thermodynamic temperature is the kelvin (K).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI base unit of amount of substance?

options.A: Mole (mol)
options.B: Candela (cd)

questions.explanation: The SI base unit of amount of substance is the mole (mol).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI base unit of luminous intensity?

options.A: Lumen (lm)
options.B: Lux (lx)

questions.explanation: The SI base unit of luminous intensity is the candela (cd).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are derived quantities?

options.A: Independent physical quantities not defined in terms of other physical quantities
options.B: Quantities obtained by combining base quantities

questions.explanation: Derived quantities are quantities obtained by combining base quantities; examples: area (m²), volume (m³), velocity (m/s), acceleration (m/s²), force (newton), pressure (pascal) and energy (joule).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of force?

options.A: Joule (J)
options.B: Watt (W)

questions.explanation: The SI unit of force is the newton (N); 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of work and energy?

options.A: Newton (N)
options.B: Joule (J)

questions.explanation: The SI unit of work and energy is the joule (J); 1 J = 1 N m = 1 kg m² s⁻².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of power?

options.A: Joule (J)
options.B: Newton (N)

questions.explanation: The SI unit of power is the watt (W); 1 W = 1 J/s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of pressure?

options.A: Newton (N)
options.B: Joule (J)

questions.explanation: The SI unit of pressure is the pascal (Pa); 1 Pa = 1 N/m².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the dimensions of velocity?

options.A: [LT]
options.B: [LT⁻¹]

questions.explanation: The dimensions of velocity are [LT⁻¹].

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the dimensions of acceleration?

options.A: [LT]
options.B: [LT⁻¹]

questions.explanation: The dimensions of acceleration are [LT⁻²].

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the dimensions of force?

options.A: [MLT⁻¹]
options.B: [MLT⁻²]

questions.explanation: The dimensions of force are [MLT⁻²].

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the dimensions of pressure?

options.A: [MLT⁻²]
options.B: [ML⁻¹T⁻²]

questions.explanation: The dimensions of pressure are [ML⁻¹T⁻²].

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is measurement?

options.A: Comparison of an unknown physical quantity with an accepted standard unit
options.B: Comparison of two unknown quantities

questions.explanation: Measurement is the comparison of an unknown physical quantity with an accepted standard unit.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instrument is used to measure very small thickness or diameter?

options.A: Metre scale
options.B: Measuring tape

questions.explanation: A screw gauge measures very small thickness or diameter. Vernier callipers measure internal/external dimensions and depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is least count?

options.A: The largest measurement an instrument can read
options.B: The smallest measurement an instrument can reliably read
options.D: The total number of divisions on a scale

questions.explanation: Least count is the smallest measurement an instrument can reliably read. Smaller least count generally means finer resolution.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a scalar quantity?

options.A: A quantity having both magnitude and direction
options.B: A quantity having magnitude only
options.D: A quantity that cannot be measured

questions.explanation: A scalar quantity has magnitude only; examples: distance, speed, mass, time, temperature, energy and work.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a vector quantity?

options.A: A quantity having magnitude only
options.B: A quantity having both magnitude and direction
options.D: A quantity that cannot be measured

questions.explanation: A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction; examples: displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, momentum and weight.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between distance and displacement?

options.A: Distance is a vector; displacement is a scalar
options.B: Distance is the total path length travelled and is a scalar; displacement is the straight-line change from initial to final position with direction and is a vector

questions.explanation: Distance is the total path length travelled and is a scalar; displacement is the straight-line change from initial to final position with direction and is a vector. Distance is never less than the magnitude of displacement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: When can displacement be zero while distance is non-zero?

options.A: When an object moves in a straight line
options.B: When an object returns to its starting point after travelling along a path
options.C: When an object is at rest
options.D: When an object moves with constant velocity

questions.explanation: Displacement can be zero while distance is non-zero when an object returns to its starting point after travelling along a path; for example, one complete lap of a circular track.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is speed?

options.A: Rate of change of displacement
options.B: Distance travelled per unit time

questions.explanation: Speed is distance travelled per unit time; average speed = total distance / total time. SI unit: m/s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is velocity?

options.A: Distance travelled per unit time
options.B: Rate of change of displacement

questions.explanation: Velocity is the rate of change of displacement; average velocity = displacement / time. SI unit: m/s. Instantaneous velocity is velocity at a particular instant.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is uniform motion?

options.A: Motion in which unequal distances are covered in equal intervals of time
options.B: Motion in which equal distances are covered in equal intervals of time, however small the intervals may be

questions.explanation: Uniform motion is motion in which equal distances are covered in equal intervals of time, however small the intervals may be.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is non-uniform motion?

options.A: Motion in which equal distances are covered in equal intervals of time
options.B: Motion in which unequal distances are covered in equal time intervals, or equal distances in unequal time intervals

questions.explanation: Non-uniform motion is motion in which unequal distances are covered in equal time intervals, or equal distances in unequal time intervals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is acceleration?

options.A: Rate of change of displacement
options.B: Rate of change of velocity with time

questions.explanation: Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity with time; a = (v - u) / t. SI unit: m/s².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is retardation or deceleration?

options.A: Acceleration in the direction of velocity
options.B: Acceleration opposite to the direction of velocity, causing the speed to decrease

questions.explanation: Retardation or deceleration is acceleration opposite to the direction of velocity, causing the speed to decrease; it is not necessarily a negative quantity in every coordinate convention.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an equation of uniformly accelerated straight-line motion?

options.A: v = u + at
options.B: v = u - at

questions.explanation: The equations of uniformly accelerated straight-line motion are: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as. Here u is initial velocity, v final velocity, a acceleration, t time and s displacement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the slope of a distance-time graph represent?

options.A: Velocity
options.B: Acceleration

questions.explanation: The slope of a distance-time graph represents speed. A steeper straight line indicates greater speed; a horizontal line indicates rest.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the slope of a displacement-time graph represent?

options.A: Speed
options.B: Velocity

questions.explanation: The slope of a displacement-time graph represents velocity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the slope of a velocity-time graph represent?

options.A: Speed
options.B: Velocity

questions.explanation: The slope of a velocity-time graph represents acceleration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?

options.A: Acceleration
options.B: Speed

questions.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph represents displacement; the signed area gives net displacement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does Newton's first law of motion state?

options.A: A body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a net external force
options.B: Net force equals rate of change of momentum
options.C: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
options.D: Energy cannot be created or destroyed

questions.explanation: Newton's first law: a body remains at rest or in uniform straight-line motion unless acted on by a net external force.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does Newton's second law of motion state?

options.A: A body remains at rest unless acted on by a net external force
options.B: Net force equals rate of change of momentum; for constant mass, F = ma
options.C: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
options.D: The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant

questions.explanation: Newton's second law: net force equals rate of change of momentum; for constant mass, F = ma.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does Newton's third law of motion state?

options.A: A body remains at rest unless acted on by a net external force
options.B: Net force equals rate of change of momentum
options.C: Every action has an equal and opposite reaction
options.D: Energy cannot be created or destroyed

questions.explanation: Newton's third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is inertia?

options.A: The tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform straight-line motion
options.B: The rate of change of momentum
options.C: The force acting on a body
options.D: The energy possessed by a body

questions.explanation: Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of rest or uniform straight-line motion. Mass is a measure of inertia.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which law of motion is called the law of inertia?

options.A: Newton's first law of motion
options.B: Newton's second law of motion

questions.explanation: Newton's first law of motion is called the law of inertia.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is momentum?

options.A: Product of mass and acceleration
options.B: Product of mass and velocity

questions.explanation: Momentum is the product of mass and velocity, p = mv. It is a vector; SI unit: kg m/s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the law of conservation of momentum?

options.A: The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant if the net external force on the system is zero
options.B: The total momentum of a system always increases
options.C: Momentum is always conserved regardless of external forces
options.D: Momentum equals force multiplied by time

questions.explanation: The total momentum of an isolated system remains constant if the net external force on the system is zero.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is force?

options.A: A push or pull that can change or tend to change an object's state of motion, direction or shape
options.B: The rate of change of displacement
options.C: The product of mass and velocity
options.D: The energy possessed by a body due to its motion

questions.explanation: Force is a push or pull that can change or tend to change an object's state of motion, direction or shape. SI unit: newton.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are contact forces?

options.A: Forces that act at a distance
options.B: Forces that require physical contact
options.C: Forces that act only in vacuum
options.D: Forces that act only on charged particles

questions.explanation: Contact forces require physical contact (friction, normal reaction, tension); non-contact forces act at a distance (gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a non-contact force?

options.A: Friction
options.B: Normal reaction

questions.explanation: Non-contact forces act at a distance; examples include gravitational, electrostatic and magnetic forces. Friction, normal reaction and tension are contact forces.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is friction?

options.A: A force that opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion between surfaces in contact
options.B: A force that acts at a distance
options.C: A force that always causes motion
options.D: A force that acts only in liquids

questions.explanation: Friction is a force that opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion between surfaces in contact. It acts along the contact surface.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a useful application of friction?

options.A: Walking
options.B: Vehicle braking

questions.explanation: Useful applications of friction include walking, vehicle braking, writing, gripping objects, lighting a match and transmitting motion through belts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can friction be reduced?

options.A: Using lubricants
options.B: Using ball bearings

questions.explanation: Friction can be reduced using lubricants, ball bearings, polishing or streamlining where appropriate.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is centripetal force?

options.A: The outward force experienced by an object in circular motion
options.B: The inward net force required to keep an object moving in a circular path; F = mv²/r
options.C: The force that opposes relative motion
options.D: The force of gravity between two masses

questions.explanation: Centripetal force is the inward net force required to keep an object moving in a circular path; F = mv²/r. It is directed towards the centre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is centrifugal force?

options.A: A real inward force in circular motion
options.B: A fictitious outward force introduced when describing motion from a rotating, non-inertial frame

questions.explanation: Centrifugal force is a fictitious outward force introduced when describing motion from a rotating, non-inertial frame; it is not an additional real interaction in an inertial frame.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is uniform circular motion?

options.A: Motion along a circular path at constant speed
options.B: Motion along a circular path at constant velocity
options.C: Motion in a straight line at constant speed

questions.explanation: Uniform circular motion is motion along a circular path at constant speed. Velocity changes continuously because its direction changes, so the body has centripetal acceleration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is gravitation?

options.A: The repulsive force between masses
options.B: The universal attractive interaction between masses

questions.explanation: Gravitation is the universal attractive interaction between masses. Newton's law gives F = Gm₁m₂/r² for point masses or spherically symmetric bodies.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate value of the universal gravitational constant G?

options.A: 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg²
options.B: 9.8 m/s²

questions.explanation: The universal gravitational constant G is approximately 6.674 × 10⁻¹¹ N m²/kg²; it is not the same as acceleration due to gravity g.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface?

options.B: 9.8 m/s²

questions.explanation: Acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface is approximately 9.8 m/s² (often rounded to 9.81 m/s²); it varies with altitude, depth, latitude and local geology.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between mass and weight?

options.A: Mass is measured in newtons; weight is measured in kilograms
options.B: Mass is the amount of matter/inertia and is measured in kg; weight is gravitational force W = mg and is measured in newtons
options.C: Mass varies with location; weight is constant

questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter/inertia and is measured in kg; weight is gravitational force W = mg and is measured in newtons. Mass is approximately constant, while weight varies with gravitational field strength.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is free fall?

options.A: Motion under the influence of gravity alone, neglecting air resistance
options.B: Motion with constant velocity
options.D: Motion under the influence of friction

questions.explanation: Free fall is motion under the influence of gravity alone, neglecting air resistance. Near Earth's surface, all bodies have the same gravitational acceleration regardless of mass.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is escape velocity?

options.A: The minimum launch speed needed to escape a body's gravitational field without further propulsion, neglecting atmosphere and other bodies
options.B: The speed of light
options.C: The speed of sound in air
options.D: The orbital speed of a satellite

questions.explanation: Escape velocity is the minimum launch speed needed to escape a body's gravitational field without further propulsion, neglecting atmosphere and other bodies. From Earth's surface it is about 11.2 km/s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is work in physics?

options.A: Work is done when a force causes displacement; W = Fs cos θ
options.B: Work is the product of mass and velocity
options.C: Work is the rate of change of momentum
options.D: Work is the product of force and time

questions.explanation: Work is done when a force causes displacement; W = Fs cos θ. SI unit: joule. Work is zero if displacement is zero or force is perpendicular to displacement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is energy?

options.A: The capacity of a system to do work or bring about change
options.B: The rate of doing work
options.C: The product of force and displacement
options.D: The product of mass and velocity

questions.explanation: Energy is the capacity of a system to do work or bring about change. SI unit: joule.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is kinetic energy?

options.A: Energy due to motion; KE = ½mv²
options.B: Energy due to position; KE = mgh

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is energy due to motion; KE = ½mv².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is potential energy?

options.A: Energy due to motion
options.B: Energy associated with position or configuration; near Earth's surface gravitational potential energy relative to a chosen level is PE = mgh

questions.explanation: Potential energy is energy associated with position or configuration. Near Earth's surface gravitational potential energy relative to a chosen level is PE = mgh.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the law of conservation of energy?

options.A: Energy can be created but not destroyed
options.B: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it is transformed or transferred, and the total energy of an isolated system remains constant
options.C: Energy can be destroyed but not created
options.D: Energy always increases in a system

questions.explanation: Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it is transformed or transferred, and the total energy of an isolated system remains constant.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is power?

options.A: Rate of doing work or transferring energy; P = W/t
options.B: Product of force and displacement

questions.explanation: Power is the rate of doing work or transferring energy; P = W/t. SI unit: watt.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a simple machine?

options.A: A device that changes the magnitude or direction of a force, or the distance through which it acts; it does not create energy
options.B: A device that creates energy
options.D: A device that only changes the direction of force

questions.explanation: A simple machine is a device that changes the magnitude or direction of a force, or the distance through which it acts; it does not create energy.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the six classical simple machines?

options.A: Lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, wedge and screw
options.B: Lever, pulley, gear, axle, wedge and screw
options.C: Lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel, wedge and nut
options.D: Lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, wedge and bolt

questions.explanation: The six classical simple machines are lever, pulley, inclined plane, wheel and axle, wedge and screw. A wedge and screw are commonly treated as forms of the inclined plane.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: In a Class I lever, where is the fulcrum located?

options.A: Between effort and load
options.B: Between fulcrum and effort

questions.explanation: Class I: fulcrum between effort and load (scissors, seesaw).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: In a Class II lever, where is the load located?

options.A: Between fulcrum and effort
options.B: Between effort and load

questions.explanation: Class II: load between fulcrum and effort (wheelbarrow, nutcracker).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: In a Class III lever, where is the effort located?

options.A: Between fulcrum and load
options.B: Between effort and load

questions.explanation: Class III: effort between fulcrum and load (tweezers, human forearm).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a pulley?

options.A: A grooved wheel with a rope or cable used to change force direction or obtain mechanical advantage
options.B: A sloping surface used to raise loads
options.C: A rigid bar that rotates about a fulcrum
options.D: A wheel rigidly attached to an axle

questions.explanation: A pulley is a grooved wheel with a rope or cable used to change force direction or obtain mechanical advantage. A fixed pulley mainly changes direction; a movable pulley can reduce the effort needed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an inclined plane?

options.A: A sloping surface used to raise or lower a load with less effort over a longer distance
options.B: A grooved wheel with a rope
options.C: A rigid bar that rotates about a fulcrum
options.D: A wheel rigidly attached to an axle

questions.explanation: An inclined plane is a sloping surface used to raise or lower a load with less effort over a longer distance; examples include ramps.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a wheel and axle?

options.A: A simple machine consisting of a larger wheel rigidly attached to a smaller axle, both rotating together
options.B: A grooved wheel with a rope
options.D: A rigid bar that rotates about a fulcrum

questions.explanation: A wheel and axle is a simple machine consisting of a larger wheel rigidly attached to a smaller axle, both rotating together; examples include a steering wheel and door knob.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is mechanical advantage (MA)?

options.A: The ratio of load to effort: MA = load / effort
options.B: The ratio of effort to load
options.C: The product of load and effort
options.D: The ratio of output work to input work

questions.explanation: Mechanical advantage (MA) is the ratio of load to effort: MA = load / effort. It is dimensionless.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the efficiency of a machine?

options.A: Efficiency = (useful output work / input work) × 100%
options.B: Efficiency = (input work / useful output work) × 100%

questions.explanation: Efficiency = (useful output work / input work) × 100%. Real machines have efficiency below 100% because of energy losses, commonly due to friction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relation among MA, velocity ratio and efficiency?

options.A: Efficiency = (MA / velocity ratio) × 100%
options.B: Efficiency = (velocity ratio / MA) × 100%

questions.explanation: Efficiency = (MA / velocity ratio) × 100%, when MA and velocity ratio are defined consistently.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the common states of matter?

options.A: Solid, liquid and gas
options.B: Solid and liquid only

questions.explanation: The common states of matter are solid, liquid and gas; plasma is another state encountered in high-energy conditions. Solids have fixed shape and volume, liquids fixed volume but no fixed shape, and gases neither fixed shape nor fixed volume.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is density?

options.A: Mass per unit volume: ρ = m/V
options.B: Volume per unit mass: ρ = V/m

questions.explanation: Density is mass per unit volume: ρ = m/V. SI unit: kg/m³.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is relative density?

options.A: The ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference substance (usually water for solids and liquids); it has no unit
options.B: The density of a substance in kg/m³
options.C: The ratio of mass to volume

questions.explanation: Relative density is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference substance (usually water for solids and liquids); it has no unit.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is pressure?

options.A: Normal force per unit area: P = F/A
options.B: Mass per unit volume

questions.explanation: Pressure is normal force per unit area: P = F/A. SI unit: pascal (Pa).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why do sharp knives cut better than blunt knives?

options.A: For the same applied force, a smaller contact area produces greater pressure
options.B: For the same applied force, a larger contact area produces greater pressure

questions.explanation: For the same applied force, a smaller contact area produces greater pressure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is standard atmospheric pressure?
questions.explanation: Standard atmospheric pressure is 101,325 Pa, equal to 1 atm or 760 mm of mercury.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which instrument measures atmospheric pressure?

options.A: Thermometer
options.B: Barometer

questions.explanation: A barometer measures atmospheric pressure; mercury and aneroid barometers are common types.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does liquid pressure vary with depth?

options.A: For a liquid of constant density at rest, gauge pressure is p = ρgh; it increases with depth and density and acts in all directions
options.B: Pressure decreases with depth
options.D: Pressure depends only on the container's shape

questions.explanation: For a liquid of constant density at rest, gauge pressure is p = ρgh; it increases with depth and density and acts in all directions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Pascal's law?

options.A: A pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid and to the container walls
options.B: Pressure in a fluid decreases with depth
options.C: The buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced
options.D: Stress is proportional to strain within the elastic limit

questions.explanation: Pascal's law: a pressure change applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid and to the container walls.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an application of Pascal's law?

options.A: Hydraulic press
options.B: Hydraulic lift

questions.explanation: Applications of Pascal's law include hydraulic press, hydraulic lift, hydraulic jack and hydraulic brakes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Archimedes' principle?

options.A: A body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced
options.B: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished
options.C: Stress is proportional to strain within the elastic limit
options.D: The total energy of an isolated system remains constant

questions.explanation: Archimedes' principle: a body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of the fluid displaced.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is buoyancy or upthrust?

options.A: The upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed or floating body
options.B: The downward force exerted by a fluid
options.C: The pressure exerted by a fluid

questions.explanation: Buoyancy or upthrust is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed or floating body.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the condition for a body to float?

options.A: A body floats when the buoyant force balances its weight
options.B: A body floats when its weight is greater than the buoyant force
options.C: A body floats when its density is greater than the fluid's density
options.D: A body floats when it is completely submerged

questions.explanation: A body floats when the buoyant force balances its weight. For a freely floating body, the weight of displaced fluid equals the body's weight.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why does an iron ship float although iron is denser than water?

options.A: Its hollow shape makes the ship's average density, including enclosed air, less than the density of water
options.B: Iron is actually less dense than water
options.C: The ship displaces less water than its weight

questions.explanation: Its hollow shape makes the ship's average density, including enclosed air, less than the density of water; it displaces enough water to balance its weight.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is surface tension?

options.A: The tangential force per unit length (or energy per unit area) at a liquid surface, arising from intermolecular forces
options.B: The resistance of a fluid to flow
options.C: The upward force exerted by a fluid
options.D: The property of a material to regain its original shape

questions.explanation: Surface tension is the tangential force per unit length (or energy per unit area) at a liquid surface, arising from intermolecular forces. SI unit: N/m.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why are small liquid drops nearly spherical?

options.A: Surface tension tends to minimise surface area for a given volume; a sphere has the minimum surface area
options.B: Gravity pulls them into a sphere
options.C: They are compressed by air pressure

questions.explanation: Surface tension tends to minimise surface area for a given volume; a sphere has the minimum surface area.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is capillarity?

options.A: Rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube due to surface tension and adhesive/cohesive forces
options.B: The resistance of a fluid to flow
options.C: The upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed body
options.D: The property of a material to regain its original shape

questions.explanation: Capillarity is the rise or fall of a liquid in a narrow tube due to surface tension and adhesive/cohesive forces; water generally rises in clean glass, while mercury is depressed.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is viscosity?

options.A: A measure of a fluid's resistance to flow or internal shear
options.B: The tangential force per unit length at a liquid surface
options.C: The upward force exerted by a fluid
options.D: The mass per unit volume of a fluid

questions.explanation: Viscosity is a measure of a fluid's resistance to flow or internal shear. SI unit of dynamic viscosity: Pa·s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is elasticity?

options.A: The property of a material to regain its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed, provided its elastic limit is not exceeded
options.B: The property of a fluid to resist flow
options.C: The tendency to minimise surface area

questions.explanation: Elasticity is the property of a material to regain its original shape and size after the deforming force is removed, provided its elastic limit is not exceeded.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Hooke's law?

options.A: Within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain; for a spring, F = -kx
options.B: Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished
options.C: The buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced
options.D: Energy cannot be created or destroyed

questions.explanation: Hooke's law: within the elastic limit, stress is proportional to strain; for a spring, F = -kx, where the minus sign indicates restoring force.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a hydraulic machine?

options.A: A machine using pressure transmitted through a confined fluid to multiply or transmit force, based on Pascal's law
options.B: A machine that uses levers
options.D: A machine that uses inclined planes

questions.explanation: A hydraulic machine is a machine using pressure transmitted through a confined fluid to multiply or transmit force, based on Pascal's law.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an everyday application of fluid mechanics?

options.A: Water supply systems
options.B: Aircraft lift

questions.explanation: Everyday applications of fluid mechanics include water supply systems, dams, aircraft lift, ship design, pumps, blood circulation, weather systems, hydraulic machinery and flow through pipes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is heat?

options.A: Energy transferred between bodies or systems because of a temperature difference
options.B: A measure of how hot or cold a body is
options.C: The total internal energy of a body
options.D: The average kinetic energy of particles

questions.explanation: Heat is energy transferred between bodies or systems because of a temperature difference. SI unit: joule (J).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is temperature?

options.A: Energy transferred due to temperature difference
options.B: A physical quantity indicating how hot or cold a body is and determining the direction of spontaneous heat transfer
options.C: The total energy of a system
options.D: The work done by a system

questions.explanation: Temperature is a physical quantity indicating how hot or cold a body is and determining the direction of spontaneous heat transfer.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between heat and temperature?

options.A: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature is a state property indicating thermal condition. Heat is measured in joules and temperature in kelvin
options.B: Heat is measured in kelvin and temperature in joules
options.C: Heat and temperature are the same
options.D: Heat is a state property and temperature is energy transferred

questions.explanation: Heat is energy transferred because of a temperature difference; temperature is a state property indicating thermal condition. Heat is measured in joules and temperature in kelvin.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of heat?

options.A: Kelvin (K)
options.B: Joule (J)

questions.explanation: The SI unit of heat is the joule (J). The calorie is a non-SI unit; one small calorie is approximately 4.184 J.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relation between Celsius and Fahrenheit scales?
questions.explanation: The relation is F = (9/5)C + 32; conversely C = (5/9)(F - 32).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relation between Celsius and Kelvin scales?
questions.explanation: The relation is K = C + 273.15.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is absolute zero?

options.A: 0 K, equal to -273.15 °C; the lower limit of thermodynamic temperature

questions.explanation: Absolute zero is 0 K, equal to -273.15 °C; it is the lower limit of thermodynamic temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of thermodynamic temperature and its correct symbol?

options.A: Kelvin, symbol K
options.B: Kelvin, symbol °K

questions.explanation: The SI unit of thermodynamic temperature is the kelvin (K); the unit name is kelvin and its symbol is K, not °K.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a thermometer?

options.A: An instrument for measuring temperature, using a temperature-dependent property such as liquid expansion, electrical resistance or thermoelectric voltage
options.B: An instrument for measuring pressure
options.C: An instrument for measuring heat capacity

questions.explanation: A thermometer is an instrument for measuring temperature, using a temperature-dependent property such as liquid expansion, electrical resistance or thermoelectric voltage.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is specific heat capacity?

options.A: The heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by one kelvin: Q = mcΔT
options.B: The heat required to change the state of unit mass of a substance
options.C: The heat required to raise the temperature of any mass by one kelvin
options.D: The total heat content of a substance

questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is the heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass of a substance by one kelvin: Q = mcΔT. SI unit: J kg⁻¹K⁻¹.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is latent heat?

options.A: Heat absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature at the phase-change condition
options.B: Heat required to raise the temperature of unit mass by one kelvin
options.C: The total heat content of a body

questions.explanation: Latent heat is heat absorbed or released during a change of state without a change in temperature at the phase-change condition. Specific latent heat is measured in J/kg.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is thermal expansion?

options.A: Increase in dimensions of a material when its temperature rises, in ordinary conditions
options.B: Decrease in dimensions of a material when its temperature rises
options.C: Change of state from solid to liquid

questions.explanation: Thermal expansion is the increase in dimensions of a material when its temperature rises, in ordinary conditions. It may be linear, area or volume expansion.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the coefficient of linear expansion?

options.A: The fractional change in length per unit temperature rise: α = ΔL/(LΔT)
options.B: The fractional change in volume per unit temperature rise
options.C: The fractional change in area per unit temperature rise
options.D: The heat required to raise temperature by one kelvin

questions.explanation: The coefficient of linear expansion is the fractional change in length per unit temperature rise: α = ΔL/(LΔT). SI unit: K⁻¹.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do solids, liquids and gases generally expand on heating?

options.A: All expand on heating; gases usually expand much more than liquids, and liquids more than solids
options.B: Solids expand most, gases least
options.D: None of them expand on heating

questions.explanation: Generally all expand on heating; gases usually expand much more than liquids, and liquids more than solids, though material-specific exceptions exist.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the anomalous expansion of water?

options.A: Water has maximum density at about 4 °C; from 0 °C to 4 °C it contracts when heated and expands when cooled
options.B: Water expands uniformly at all temperatures

questions.explanation: Water has maximum density at about 4 °C; from 0 °C to 4 °C it contracts when heated and expands when cooled. This is the anomalous expansion of water.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is melting?

options.A: Change of state from solid to liquid by absorbing heat at the melting point
options.B: Change of state from liquid to solid
options.C: Change of state from liquid to gas
options.D: Change of state from solid to gas

questions.explanation: Melting is the change of state from solid to liquid by absorbing heat at the melting point (for a pure substance at a specified pressure).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is freezing?

options.A: Change of state from liquid to solid; it releases latent heat
options.B: Change of state from solid to liquid
options.C: Change of state from liquid to gas
options.D: Change of state from gas to solid

questions.explanation: Freezing is the change of state from liquid to solid; it releases latent heat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is evaporation?

options.A: A surface phenomenon in which molecules escape from a liquid at temperatures below its boiling point; it causes cooling
options.B: Rapid vaporisation throughout a liquid at its boiling point
options.D: Direct change from solid to gas

questions.explanation: Evaporation is a surface phenomenon in which molecules escape from a liquid at temperatures below its boiling point; it causes cooling.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is condensation?

options.A: Change of gas or vapour into liquid, generally releasing latent heat
options.B: Change of liquid into gas

questions.explanation: Condensation is the change of gas or vapour into liquid, generally releasing latent heat.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is boiling?

options.A: Rapid vaporisation throughout a liquid when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure
options.B: Surface evaporation at any temperature
options.D: Direct change from solid to gas

questions.explanation: Boiling is rapid vaporisation throughout a liquid when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure; the boiling point changes with pressure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is sublimation?

options.A: Direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state
options.B: Change from solid to liquid

questions.explanation: Sublimation is the direct change from solid to gas without passing through the liquid state; examples include dry ice and naphthalene under suitable conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the three modes of heat transfer?

options.A: Conduction, convection and radiation
options.B: Evaporation, condensation and sublimation

questions.explanation: The three modes of heat transfer are conduction, convection and radiation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is conduction?

options.A: Transfer of heat through a material without bulk movement of the material
options.B: Transfer of heat by bulk movement of a fluid
options.C: Transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves

questions.explanation: Conduction is the transfer of heat through a material without bulk movement of the material; it is especially effective in solids and metals are generally good conductors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is convection?

options.A: Transfer of heat by bulk movement of a fluid, driven by density differences or forced flow
options.B: Transfer of heat through a material without bulk movement
options.C: Transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves

questions.explanation: Convection is the transfer of heat by bulk movement of a fluid (liquid or gas), driven by density differences or forced flow.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is radiation?

options.A: Transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves; it requires no material medium and can occur through a vacuum
options.B: Transfer of heat through a material without bulk movement
options.C: Transfer of heat by bulk movement of a fluid

questions.explanation: Radiation is the transfer of energy by electromagnetic waves; it requires no material medium and can occur through a vacuum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is thermal insulation?

options.A: Use of materials or design features that reduce heat transfer; examples include fibreglass, foam, trapped air and double glazing
options.B: Use of materials that increase heat transfer
options.D: Change of state from solid to liquid

questions.explanation: Thermal insulation is the use of materials or design features that reduce heat transfer; examples include fibreglass, foam, trapped air and double glazing.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the physical principle behind the greenhouse effect?

options.A: Certain gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation, reducing the rate at which Earth loses heat to space and warming the surface and lower atmosphere
options.B: Certain gases reflect all sunlight back to space
options.C: The ozone layer traps all heat

questions.explanation: Certain gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation, reducing the rate at which Earth loses heat to space and warming the surface and lower atmosphere.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the zeroth law of thermodynamics state?

options.A: Thermal equilibrium is transitive and defines temperature
options.B: Energy is conserved
options.C: Entropy of an isolated system never decreases
options.D: Entropy approaches a constant minimum as temperature approaches 0 K

questions.explanation: Zeroth law: thermal equilibrium is transitive and defines temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the first law of thermodynamics state?

options.A: Energy is conserved (ΔU = Q - W when W is work done by the system)
options.B: Heat does not spontaneously flow from cold to hot
options.C: Entropy of an isolated system never decreases
options.D: Entropy approaches a constant minimum as temperature approaches 0 K

questions.explanation: First law: energy is conserved (ΔU = Q - W when W is work done by the system).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the second law of thermodynamics state?

options.A: Entropy of an isolated system never decreases; heat does not spontaneously flow from cold to hot
options.B: Energy is conserved
options.D: Entropy approaches a constant minimum as temperature approaches 0 K

questions.explanation: Second law: entropy of an isolated system never decreases; heat does not spontaneously flow from cold to hot.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What does the third law of thermodynamics state?

options.A: Entropy approaches a constant minimum for a perfect crystal as temperature approaches 0 K
options.B: Energy is conserved
options.C: Heat does not spontaneously flow from cold to hot

questions.explanation: Third law: entropy approaches a constant minimum for a perfect crystal as temperature approaches 0 K.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is internal energy?

options.A: The microscopic kinetic and potential energy of the particles in a system; it is a state function
options.B: The energy transferred due to temperature difference
options.C: The work done by a system
options.D: The total energy of an isolated system

questions.explanation: Internal energy is the microscopic kinetic and potential energy of the particles in a system; it is a state function.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a heat engine?

options.A: A device that absorbs heat from a high-temperature source, converts part of it into work and rejects the remainder to a lower-temperature sink
options.B: A device that converts work entirely into heat
options.C: A device that transfers heat from cold to hot without work

questions.explanation: A heat engine is a device that absorbs heat from a high-temperature source, converts part of it into work and rejects the remainder to a lower-temperature sink.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Can a heat engine convert all absorbed heat into work in a cyclic process?

options.A: No, the second law of thermodynamics prevents a cyclic heat engine from converting all input heat into work; some heat must be rejected
options.B: Yes, if the engine is ideal
options.C: Yes, if there is no friction

questions.explanation: No. The second law of thermodynamics prevents a cyclic heat engine from converting all input heat into work; some heat must be rejected.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a refrigerator?

options.A: A device that uses external work to transfer heat from a low-temperature region to a higher-temperature surrounding
options.B: A device that converts heat entirely into work
options.D: A device that produces heat from work

questions.explanation: A refrigerator is a device that uses external work to transfer heat from a low-temperature region to a higher-temperature surrounding.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an air conditioner?

options.A: A refrigeration system that removes heat from indoor air and rejects it outside; it commonly also controls humidity and air circulation
options.B: A device that converts heat entirely into work
options.D: A device that produces electricity from heat

questions.explanation: An air conditioner is a refrigeration system that removes heat from indoor air and rejects it outside; it commonly also controls humidity and air circulation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the coefficient of performance (COP) of a refrigerator?

options.A: COP = heat removed from the cold space / work input
options.B: COP = work input / heat removed from the cold space

questions.explanation: COP = heat removed from the cold space / work input. It is not the same as thermal efficiency.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the two types of electric charge?

options.A: Positive and negative
options.B: North and south

questions.explanation: The two types of electric charge are positive and negative. Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relative charge of an electron?
questions.explanation: The charge of an electron is -1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The neutron has zero net electric charge.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the charge of a proton?
questions.explanation: The charge of a proton is +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the net electric charge of a neutron?
questions.explanation: The neutron has zero net electric charge.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is static electricity?

options.A: Accumulation or imbalance of electric charge on an object's surface or within an insulating material
options.B: Flow of electric charge through a conductor
options.C: The work done per unit charge

questions.explanation: Static electricity is the accumulation or imbalance of electric charge on an object's surface or within an insulating material.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can an object be charged?

options.A: By friction
options.B: By conduction (contact)

questions.explanation: An object can be charged by friction, conduction (contact) or induction (redistribution without direct contact, usually with grounding to leave a net charge).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electric current?

options.A: Rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q/t for steady current
options.B: Work done per unit charge
options.D: The energy transferred by electric current

questions.explanation: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge: I = Q/t for steady current. SI unit: ampere (A).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is conventional current?

options.A: The defined direction of positive charge flow, from higher to lower potential in an external circuit; in metal wires it is opposite to electron drift
options.B: The flow of electrons from higher to lower potential
options.C: The flow of positive charges in metal wires
options.D: The flow of current in a superconductor

questions.explanation: Conventional current is the defined direction of positive charge flow, from higher to lower potential in an external circuit; in metal wires it is opposite to electron drift.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is potential difference (voltage)?

options.A: Work done per unit charge in moving charge between two points: V = W/Q
options.B: Rate of flow of electric charge
options.D: The energy transferred by electric current

questions.explanation: Potential difference (voltage) is the work done per unit charge in moving charge between two points: V = W/Q. SI unit: volt (V).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electrical resistance?

options.A: Opposition offered by a component to electric current; R = V/I for an ohmic conductor
options.B: Rate of flow of electric charge
options.D: The energy transferred by electric current

questions.explanation: Electrical resistance is the opposition offered by a component to electric current. R = V/I for an ohmic conductor; SI unit: ohm (Ω).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a conductor?

options.A: Copper
options.B: Rubber

questions.explanation: Conductors allow charge to move relatively easily (copper, aluminium); insulators strongly resist charge flow (rubber, glass, dry plastic).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an insulator?

options.A: Aluminium
options.B: Rubber

questions.explanation: Insulators strongly resist charge flow (rubber, glass, dry plastic).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Ohm's law?

options.A: For a conductor under constant physical conditions, current is directly proportional to potential difference: V = IR
options.B: Current is inversely proportional to potential difference
options.C: Resistance is directly proportional to current
options.D: Voltage is directly proportional to resistance

questions.explanation: Ohm's law: for a conductor under constant physical conditions, current is directly proportional to potential difference: V = IR.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electrical resistivity?

options.A: A material property defined by ρ = RA/L for a uniform conductor
options.B: The opposition offered by a component to electric current
options.C: The rate of flow of electric charge
options.D: The work done per unit charge

questions.explanation: Electrical resistivity is a material property defined by ρ = RA/L for a uniform conductor. SI unit: ohm metre (Ω m). Resistance depends on length, cross-sectional area, material and temperature.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are resistors connected in series?

options.A: The same current flows through each resistor; equivalent resistance R = R₁ + R₂ + ...; voltage divides across them
options.B: The same voltage is across each resistor
options.C: The equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance

questions.explanation: In series, the same current flows through each resistor; equivalent resistance R = R₁ + R₂ + ...; voltage divides across them.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are resistors connected in parallel?

options.A: The same voltage is across each branch; 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...; equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual branch resistance
options.B: The same current flows through each branch
options.C: The equivalent resistance is the sum of individual resistances
options.D: The voltage divides across each branch

questions.explanation: In parallel, the same voltage is across each branch; 1/R = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...; equivalent resistance is less than the smallest individual branch resistance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electric power?

options.A: Rate of electrical energy transfer: P = VI = I²R = V²/R for an ohmic resistor
options.B: The total electrical energy transferred
options.D: The work done per unit charge

questions.explanation: Electric power is the rate of electrical energy transfer: P = VI = I²R = V²/R for an ohmic resistor. SI unit: watt.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electrical energy?

options.A: Energy transferred by electric current; E = Pt = VIt
options.B: The rate of electrical energy transfer
options.D: The work done per unit charge

questions.explanation: Electrical energy is energy transferred by electric current; E = Pt = VIt. SI unit: joule; household billing commonly uses kilowatt-hour.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Joule's law of heating?

options.A: Heat produced in a resistor is H = I²Rt
options.B: Heat produced in a resistor is H = IRt
options.C: Heat produced in a resistor is H = I²R/t
options.D: Heat produced in a resistor is H = IR²t

questions.explanation: Joule's law of heating: heat produced in a resistor is H = I²Rt, also H = VIt or V²t/R for an ohmic resistor under the relevant conditions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an application of the heating effect of current?

options.A: Electric iron
options.B: Electric heater

questions.explanation: Applications of the heating effect of current include electric iron, heater, toaster, kettle, incandescent filament and fuse wire.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the magnetic effect of electric current?

options.A: An electric current produces a magnetic field around the conductor
options.B: A magnetic field produces an electric current

questions.explanation: The magnetic effect of electric current: an electric current produces a magnetic field around the conductor; this is the operating principle behind electromagnets and electric motors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an electric fuse?

options.A: A sacrificial safety device containing a low-melting-point element that melts and breaks the circuit when excessive current flows
options.B: A device that automatically opens a circuit during overcurrent and can be reset
options.C: A device that connects exposed conductive parts to earth
options.D: A device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy

questions.explanation: An electric fuse is a sacrificial safety device containing a low-melting-point element that melts and breaks the circuit when excessive current flows.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an MCB?

options.A: A miniature circuit breaker that automatically opens a circuit during overcurrent due to overload or short circuit and can generally be reset after the fault is cleared
options.B: A sacrificial safety device that melts when excessive current flows
options.C: A device that connects exposed conductive parts to earth
options.D: A device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy

questions.explanation: An MCB (miniature circuit breaker) automatically opens a circuit during overcurrent due to overload or short circuit and can generally be reset after the fault is cleared.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is earthing?

options.A: Connecting exposed conductive parts of electrical equipment to earth through a low-resistance protective path so fault current can flow safely and protective devices can operate
options.B: Connecting electrical equipment to a high-voltage source
options.C: A sacrificial safety device that melts when excessive current flows
options.D: A device that automatically opens a circuit during overcurrent

questions.explanation: Earthing is connecting exposed conductive parts of electrical equipment to earth through a low-resistance protective path so fault current can flow safely and protective devices can operate.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a short circuit?

options.A: An unintended low-resistance connection between points of different potential, causing a very large current
options.B: Drawing more current from a circuit than its rated capacity
options.C: Connecting exposed conductive parts to earth
options.D: A device that automatically opens a circuit during overcurrent

questions.explanation: A short circuit is an unintended low-resistance connection between points of different potential, causing a very large current.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is overloading?

options.A: Drawing more current from a circuit than its rated capacity, often by connecting too many or high-power appliances
options.B: An unintended low-resistance connection between points of different potential
options.C: Connecting exposed conductive parts to earth
options.D: A device that automatically opens a circuit during overcurrent

questions.explanation: Overloading is drawing more current from a circuit than its rated capacity, often by connecting too many or high-power appliances.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How are household electrical appliances generally connected?

options.A: In parallel so each receives the supply voltage and can operate independently
options.B: In series so the same current flows through each
options.C: In a combination of series and parallel

questions.explanation: Household appliances are connected in parallel so each receives the supply voltage and can operate independently; live, neutral and earth conductors have distinct safety functions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between AC and DC?

options.A: Alternating current (AC) periodically reverses direction; direct current (DC) flows in one direction
options.B: AC flows in one direction; DC periodically reverses direction

questions.explanation: Alternating current (AC) periodically reverses direction; direct current (DC) flows in one direction. Mains electricity is AC; batteries supply DC.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is one kilowatt-hour?

options.A: The energy used by a 1 kW device operating for 1 hour; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J
options.B: The power used by a 1 kW device operating for 1 hour
options.C: The energy used by a 1 W device operating for 1 hour
options.D: The energy used by a 1 kW device operating for 1 second

questions.explanation: One kilowatt-hour is the energy used by a 1 kW device operating for 1 hour; 1 kWh = 3.6 × 10⁶ J. It is a unit of energy, not power.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is electricity consumption calculated?

options.A: Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours
options.B: Energy in kWh = power in W × time in hours
options.C: Energy in kWh = power in kW / time in hours
options.D: Energy in kWh = power in W / time in hours

questions.explanation: Energy in kWh = power in kW × time in hours. Example: a 100 W device used for 10 hours consumes 1 kWh.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are natural and artificial magnets?

options.A: Natural magnets occur in nature, such as lodestone (magnetite); artificial magnets are manufactured in desired shapes and strengths
options.B: Natural magnets are manufactured; artificial magnets occur in nature

questions.explanation: Natural magnets occur in nature, such as lodestone (magnetite); artificial magnets are manufactured in desired shapes and strengths.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are magnetic poles?

options.A: The regions of a magnet where magnetic effects are strongest, called north-seeking and south-seeking poles
options.B: The regions of a magnet where magnetic effects are weakest
options.D: The regions of a magnet where there is no magnetic effect

questions.explanation: Magnetic poles are the regions of a magnet where magnetic effects are strongest, called north-seeking and south-seeking poles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the basic property of magnets regarding poles?

options.A: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract
options.B: Like poles attract and unlike poles repel

questions.explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract; a freely suspended magnet aligns approximately north-south; magnetic poles always occur in pairs in ordinary magnets.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Can a magnetic pole exist alone?

options.A: No isolated magnetic monopole has been observed; cutting a magnet produces smaller magnets, each with north and south poles
options.B: Yes, a north pole can exist alone
options.C: Yes, a south pole can exist alone

questions.explanation: No isolated magnetic monopole has been observed; cutting a magnet produces smaller magnets, each with north and south poles.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a magnetic field?

options.A: The region in which a magnetic pole, magnet or moving charge/current experiences magnetic force
options.B: The region in which an electric charge experiences electric force
options.C: The region in which a mass experiences gravitational force
options.D: The region in which a body experiences frictional force

questions.explanation: A magnetic field is the region in which a magnetic pole, magnet or moving charge/current experiences magnetic force.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are magnetic field lines?

options.A: Imaginary curves whose tangent gives the field direction; outside a bar magnet they run from north to south, form closed loops, and never intersect
options.B: Imaginary curves that run from south to north outside a magnet
options.C: Imaginary curves that can intersect each other
options.D: Imaginary curves that are always straight lines

questions.explanation: Magnetic field lines are imaginary curves whose tangent gives the field direction; outside a bar magnet they run from north to south, form closed loops, and never intersect.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Earth's magnetism?

options.A: Earth behaves approximately like a giant magnet, producing a magnetic field that helps a compass align; magnetic and geographic poles are not identical
options.B: Earth does not have a magnetic field
options.C: Earth's magnetic poles are exactly at the geographic poles
options.D: Earth's magnetic field is produced by electric currents in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: Earth behaves approximately like a giant magnet, producing a magnetic field that helps a compass align; magnetic and geographic poles are not identical.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a magnetic compass?

options.A: A device with a freely rotating magnetised needle that aligns approximately with Earth's local magnetic field
options.B: A device that measures electric current
options.C: A device that measures atmospheric pressure

questions.explanation: A magnetic compass is a device with a freely rotating magnetised needle that aligns approximately with Earth's local magnetic field.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which materials are strongly attracted by magnets?

options.A: Ferromagnetic materials such as iron, cobalt and nickel, and some of their alloys
options.B: Diamagnetic materials such as copper and gold
options.C: Paramagnetic materials such as aluminium and platinum
options.D: Non-magnetic materials such as wood and plastic

questions.explanation: Ferromagnetic materials such as iron, cobalt and nickel, and some of their alloys, are strongly attracted by magnets.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an electromagnet?

options.A: A temporary magnet produced by electric current, usually by winding a coil around a soft-iron core
options.B: A permanent magnet made of steel
options.C: A natural magnet such as lodestone
options.D: A device that measures magnetic field

questions.explanation: An electromagnet is a temporary magnet produced by electric current, usually by winding a coil around a soft-iron core.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can the strength of an electromagnet be increased?

options.A: Increase the current
options.B: Increase the number of coil turns
options.C: Use a suitable high-permeability core such as soft iron

questions.explanation: The strength of an electromagnet can be increased by increasing the current, increasing the number of coil turns, or using a suitable high-permeability core such as soft iron.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is electromagnetic induction?

options.A: Production of an electromotive force (and current in a closed circuit) when magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes
options.B: Production of a magnetic field by an electric current
options.C: Production of heat by an electric current
options.D: Production of light by an electric current

questions.explanation: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force (and current in a closed circuit) when magnetic flux linked with a circuit changes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction?

options.A: The induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage; for a coil, ε = -N dΦ/dt
options.B: The induced EMF is proportional to the magnetic flux
options.C: The induced EMF is inversely proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux
options.D: The induced EMF is proportional to the current

questions.explanation: Faraday's law: the induced EMF is proportional to the rate of change of magnetic flux linkage; for a coil, ε = -N dΦ/dt. The negative sign represents Lenz's law.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an electric motor?

options.A: A device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy using the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field
options.B: A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy
options.C: A device that converts electrical energy into heat
options.D: A device that converts light into electrical energy

questions.explanation: An electric motor converts electrical energy into mechanical energy using the force on a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an electric generator?

options.A: A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction
options.B: A device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy
options.C: A device that converts electrical energy into heat
options.D: A device that converts light into electrical energy

questions.explanation: An electric generator converts mechanical energy into electrical energy by electromagnetic induction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a transformer?

options.A: A device that transfers AC electrical energy between circuits by mutual induction and changes voltage/current levels; it does not operate on steady DC in normal operation
options.B: A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy
options.C: A device that converts electrical energy into mechanical energy
options.D: A device that converts AC into DC

questions.explanation: A transformer transfers AC electrical energy between circuits by mutual induction and changes voltage/current levels; it does not operate on steady DC in normal operation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the principle of a transformer?

options.A: Mutual electromagnetic induction
options.B: Self-induction

questions.explanation: The principle of a transformer is mutual electromagnetic induction. For an ideal transformer, V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a step-up transformer?

options.A: A transformer with more turns in the secondary coil than in the primary; it increases voltage and decreases current for approximately conserved power
options.B: A transformer with fewer turns in the secondary coil than in the primary
options.C: A transformer with equal turns in both coils
options.D: A transformer that converts AC into DC

questions.explanation: A step-up transformer has more turns in the secondary coil than in the primary; it increases voltage and decreases current for approximately conserved power.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a step-down transformer?

options.A: A transformer with fewer turns in the secondary coil than in the primary; it decreases voltage and increases current
options.B: A transformer with more turns in the secondary coil than in the primary
options.C: A transformer with equal turns in both coils
options.D: A transformer that converts AC into DC

questions.explanation: A step-down transformer has fewer turns in the secondary coil than in the primary; it decreases voltage and increases current.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Why is electricity transmitted at high voltage?

options.A: For a given transmitted power, higher voltage means lower current; resistive line loss I²R is therefore reduced
options.B: Higher voltage means higher current, which reduces loss
options.C: Higher voltage increases the resistance of transmission lines
options.D: Higher voltage reduces the power transmitted

questions.explanation: For a given transmitted power, higher voltage means lower current; resistive line loss I²R is therefore reduced.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between AC and DC generators?

options.A: An AC generator produces alternating output; a DC generator uses a commutator to deliver unidirectional output at its terminals
options.B: An AC generator uses a commutator; a DC generator does not

questions.explanation: An AC generator produces alternating output; a DC generator uses a commutator to deliver unidirectional output at its terminals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an application of electromagnetism?

options.A: Electric motors
options.B: Transformers

questions.explanation: Applications of electromagnetism include electric motors, generators, transformers, relays, loudspeakers, electric bells, MRI systems, induction cooktops and electromagnetic cranes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is light?

options.A: Visible light is electromagnetic radiation detectable by the human eye; in vacuum it travels at approximately 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s
options.B: A mechanical wave that requires a medium

questions.explanation: Visible light is electromagnetic radiation detectable by the human eye; in vacuum it travels at approximately 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is rectilinear propagation of light?

options.A: The principle that light travels in straight lines through a homogeneous transparent medium
options.B: The principle that light bends around obstacles
options.C: The principle that light travels in curved paths
options.D: The principle that light requires a medium

questions.explanation: Rectilinear propagation of light is the principle that light travels in straight lines through a homogeneous transparent medium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is reflection of light?

options.A: The return of light into the original medium after it strikes a surface
options.B: The bending of light when it passes between media
