options.C: The splitting of white light into colours
options.D: The complete reflection back into the denser medium

questions.explanation: Reflection of light is the return of light into the original medium after it strikes a surface.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the laws of reflection?

options.A: The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
options.B: The incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in different planes
options.C: The angle of incidence is greater than the angle of reflection
options.D: The angle of incidence is less than the angle of reflection

questions.explanation: Laws of reflection: the incident ray, reflected ray and normal lie in the same plane; the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What type of image is formed by a plane mirror?

options.A: Virtual, erect, same size as the object, laterally inverted and at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front
options.B: Real, inverted and diminished

questions.explanation: A plane mirror forms a virtual, erect, same-size image that is laterally inverted and at the same distance behind the mirror as the object is in front.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a spherical mirror?

options.A: A mirror whose reflecting surface forms part of a sphere; it may be concave or convex
options.B: A mirror with a flat reflecting surface
options.C: A mirror with a cylindrical reflecting surface
options.D: A mirror with a parabolic reflecting surface

questions.explanation: A spherical mirror is a mirror whose reflecting surface forms part of a sphere; it may be concave or convex.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a concave mirror?

options.A: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves inward; it can form real or virtual images depending on object position
options.B: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface bulges outward
options.C: A mirror with a flat reflecting surface
options.D: A mirror that always forms virtual images

questions.explanation: A concave mirror is a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves inward. It can form real or virtual images depending on object position and is used in shaving/makeup mirrors, headlights and reflecting telescopes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a convex mirror?

options.A: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface bulges outward; it always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image
options.B: A spherical mirror whose reflecting surface curves inward
options.C: A mirror with a flat reflecting surface
options.D: A mirror that always forms real images

questions.explanation: A convex mirror is a spherical mirror whose reflecting surface bulges outward; it always forms a virtual, erect and diminished image and is used as a rear-view mirror.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the mirror formula?

options.A: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u using the Cartesian sign convention
options.B: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u using the Cartesian sign convention
options.D: f = v + u using the Cartesian sign convention

questions.explanation: The mirror formula is 1/f = 1/v + 1/u using the Cartesian sign convention; f is focal length, v image distance and u object distance.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is magnification for a spherical mirror?

options.A: m = h_i/h_o = -v/u under the Cartesian sign convention
options.B: m = h_i/h_o = v/u under the Cartesian sign convention
options.C: m = h_i/h_o = -u/v under the Cartesian sign convention
options.D: m = h_i/h_o = u/v under the Cartesian sign convention

questions.explanation: Magnification for a spherical mirror is m = h_i/h_o = -v/u under the Cartesian sign convention.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is refraction?

options.A: Change in direction of light when it passes obliquely between media because its speed changes
options.B: The return of light into the original medium after it strikes a surface
options.C: The splitting of white light into colours
options.D: The complete reflection back into the denser medium

questions.explanation: Refraction is the change in direction of light when it passes obliquely between media because its speed changes.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the laws of refraction?

options.A: The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane; for a given pair of media, n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r (Snell's law)
options.B: The incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in different planes
options.C: The angle of incidence is always greater than the angle of refraction
options.D: The angle of incidence is always less than the angle of refraction

questions.explanation: Laws of refraction: the incident ray, refracted ray and normal lie in the same plane; for a given pair of media, n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r (Snell's law).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is refractive index?

options.A: For a medium, absolute refractive index n = c/v, where c is speed of light in vacuum and v is its phase speed in the medium
options.B: The ratio of the speed of light in the medium to the speed of light in vacuum
options.C: The ratio of the frequency of light in vacuum to the frequency in the medium
options.D: The ratio of the wavelength of light in the medium to the wavelength in vacuum

questions.explanation: Refractive index: for a medium, absolute refractive index n = c/v, where c is speed of light in vacuum and v is its phase speed in the medium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is total internal reflection?

options.A: Complete reflection back into the denser medium when light travels from optically denser to rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
options.B: Complete reflection back into the rarer medium when light travels from optically rarer to denser medium
options.C: Partial reflection at the boundary between two media
options.D: The splitting of white light into colours

questions.explanation: Total internal reflection is complete reflection back into the denser medium when light travels from optically denser to rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What conditions are required for total internal reflection?

options.A: Light must travel from higher to lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle
options.B: Light must travel from lower to higher refractive index, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle
options.C: Light must travel from higher to lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence must be less than the critical angle
options.D: Light must travel from lower to higher refractive index, and the angle of incidence must be less than the critical angle

questions.explanation: Conditions for total internal reflection: light must travel from higher to lower refractive index, and the angle of incidence must exceed the critical angle.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is dispersion of light?

options.A: Separation of white light into component colours because refractive index depends on wavelength
options.B: The bending of light when it passes between media
options.C: The return of light into the original medium
options.D: The complete reflection back into the denser medium

questions.explanation: Dispersion of light is the separation of white light into component colours because refractive index depends on wavelength; violet generally deviates more than red in a prism.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the visible spectrum order?

options.A: Violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR)
options.B: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet (ROYGBIV)
options.C: Violet, blue, green, yellow, red, indigo and orange
options.D: Red, yellow, green, blue, violet, indigo and orange

questions.explanation: The visible spectrum order is violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR); red has the longest wavelength and violet the shortest in visible light.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is a rainbow formed?

options.A: Mainly by refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets; the primary rainbow has red on the outer edge and violet on the inner edge
options.B: By reflection of sunlight from a mirror
options.C: By refraction of sunlight through a glass prism
options.D: By diffraction of sunlight around water droplets

questions.explanation: A rainbow is formed mainly by refraction, dispersion and internal reflection of sunlight in water droplets; the primary rainbow has red on the outer edge and violet on the inner edge.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a lens?

options.A: A transparent optical element that refracts light to converge or diverge rays; common types are convex and concave lenses
options.B: A mirror whose reflecting surface forms part of a sphere
options.C: A device that splits white light into colours
options.D: A device that measures light intensity

questions.explanation: A lens is a transparent optical element that refracts light to converge or diverge rays; common types are convex and concave lenses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a convex lens?

options.A: A converging lens, thicker at the centre than at the edges in the usual form; it can form real or virtual images depending on object position
options.B: A diverging lens, thinner at the centre than at the edges
options.C: A lens with a flat surface
options.D: A lens that always forms virtual images

questions.explanation: A convex lens is a converging lens, thicker at the centre than at the edges in the usual form; it can form real or virtual images depending on object position.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a concave lens?

options.A: A diverging lens, thinner at the centre than at the edges in the usual form; for a real object it forms a virtual, erect and diminished image
options.B: A converging lens, thicker at the centre than at the edges
options.C: A lens with a flat surface
options.D: A lens that always forms real images

questions.explanation: A concave lens is a diverging lens, thinner at the centre than at the edges in the usual form; for a real object it forms a virtual, erect and diminished image.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the thin-lens formula?

options.A: 1/f = 1/v - 1/u under the Cartesian sign convention
options.B: 1/f = 1/v + 1/u under the Cartesian sign convention
options.D: f = v - u under the Cartesian sign convention

questions.explanation: The thin-lens formula is 1/f = 1/v - 1/u under the Cartesian sign convention.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the power of a lens?

options.A: P = 1/f when focal length f is in metres; SI-derived practical unit is dioptre (D), equal to m⁻¹
options.B: P = f when focal length f is in metres
options.C: P = 1/f when focal length f is in centimetres
options.D: P = f² when focal length f is in metres

questions.explanation: Power of a lens: P = 1/f when focal length f is in metres; SI-derived practical unit is dioptre (D), equal to m⁻¹. Convex lens power is positive and concave lens power negative.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following are main parts of the human eye?

options.A: Cornea, aqueous humour, iris, pupil, crystalline lens, ciliary muscles, vitreous humour, retina, optic nerve and sclera
options.B: Cornea, iris, pupil and retina only
options.C: Lens, retina and optic nerve only

questions.explanation: The main parts of the human eye include cornea, aqueous humour, iris, pupil, crystalline lens, ciliary muscles, vitreous humour, retina, optic nerve and sclera.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does the human eye form an image?

options.A: The cornea and lens refract light to focus a real, inverted and diminished image on the retina; the brain interprets the signals
options.B: The cornea and lens refract light to focus a virtual, erect and magnified image on the retina
options.C: The eye forms a real, erect and magnified image on the retina
options.D: The eye forms a virtual, inverted and diminished image on the retina

questions.explanation: The cornea and lens refract light to focus a real, inverted and diminished image on the retina; the brain interprets the signals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is accommodation of the eye?

options.A: The ability of the eye lens to change its curvature and focal length, through ciliary muscles, to focus objects at different distances
options.B: The ability of the eye to adapt to different light intensities
options.C: The ability of the eye to perceive colours
options.D: The ability of the eye to perceive depth

questions.explanation: Accommodation of the eye is the ability of the eye lens to change its curvature and focal length, through ciliary muscles, to focus objects at different distances.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the near point of a normal adult eye?

options.A: Approximately 25 cm
options.B: Approximately 2.5 cm

questions.explanation: The near point of a normal adult eye is approximately 25 cm; it can vary with age and individual.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is myopia?

options.A: Short-sightedness: distant objects appear blurred because images focus in front of the retina; corrected using a concave (diverging) lens
options.B: Long-sightedness: nearby objects appear blurred because images would focus behind the retina
options.D: A refractive error caused by unequal curvature of the cornea

questions.explanation: Myopia is short-sightedness: distant objects appear blurred because images focus in front of the retina; corrected using a concave (diverging) lens.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is hypermetropia?

options.A: Long-sightedness: nearby objects appear blurred because images would focus behind the retina; corrected using a convex (converging) lens
options.B: Short-sightedness: distant objects appear blurred because images focus in front of the retina
options.D: A refractive error caused by unequal curvature of the cornea

questions.explanation: Hypermetropia is long-sightedness: nearby objects appear blurred because images would focus behind the retina; corrected using a convex (converging) lens.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is presbyopia?

options.A: Age-related reduction in accommodation, commonly due to reduced lens flexibility; corrected with suitable convex reading lenses, bifocals or progressive lenses
options.B: Short-sightedness
options.D: A refractive error caused by unequal curvature of the cornea

questions.explanation: Presbyopia is age-related reduction in accommodation, commonly due to reduced lens flexibility; corrected with suitable convex reading lenses, bifocals or progressive lenses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is astigmatism?

options.A: A refractive error caused by unequal curvature/power in different meridians of the cornea or lens; corrected with cylindrical or toric lenses
options.B: Short-sightedness

questions.explanation: Astigmatism is a refractive error caused by unequal curvature/power in different meridians of the cornea or lens; corrected with cylindrical or toric lenses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a microscope?

options.A: An optical instrument used to view small nearby objects with magnification; a compound microscope uses objective and eyepiece lenses
options.B: An instrument used to view distant objects
options.C: An instrument that allows viewing over or around obstacles
options.D: An instrument that measures light intensity

questions.explanation: A microscope is an optical instrument used to view small nearby objects with magnification; a compound microscope uses objective and eyepiece lenses.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a telescope?

options.A: An instrument used to view distant objects; an astronomical refracting telescope commonly uses an objective and an eyepiece
options.B: An instrument used to view small nearby objects
options.C: An instrument that allows viewing over or around obstacles
options.D: An instrument that measures light intensity

questions.explanation: A telescope is an instrument used to view distant objects; an astronomical refracting telescope commonly uses an objective and an eyepiece.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a camera?

options.A: An optical device in which a lens forms a real image on a film or electronic image sensor; focusing changes lens-sensor geometry or lens position
options.B: An instrument used to view distant objects
options.C: An instrument used to view small nearby objects
options.D: An instrument that allows viewing over or around obstacles

questions.explanation: A camera is an optical device in which a lens forms a real image on a film or electronic image sensor; focusing changes lens-sensor geometry or lens position.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a periscope?

options.A: An optical instrument that allows viewing over or around obstacles, commonly using two plane mirrors or prisms
options.B: An instrument used to view distant objects
options.C: An instrument used to view small nearby objects
options.D: An instrument that measures light intensity

questions.explanation: A periscope is an optical instrument that allows viewing over or around obstacles, commonly using two plane mirrors or prisms.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are binoculars?

options.A: A pair of compact telescopes, one for each eye, that provide stereoscopic viewing and depth perception
options.B: A single telescope used with one eye
options.C: An instrument used to view small nearby objects
options.D: An instrument that allows viewing over or around obstacles

questions.explanation: Binoculars are a pair of compact telescopes, one for each eye, that provide stereoscopic viewing and depth perception.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is fibre optics?

options.A: Transmission of light through thin transparent fibres by repeated total internal reflection; used in telecommunications, medical endoscopy and sensors
options.B: Transmission of light through a vacuum
options.C: Transmission of light through a glass prism by dispersion
options.D: Transmission of light through a lens by refraction

questions.explanation: Fibre optics is the transmission of light through thin transparent fibres by repeated total internal reflection; used in telecommunications, medical endoscopy and sensors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a laser?

options.A: A source of light produced by stimulated emission; laser light is typically highly directional, coherent and narrow in wavelength range
options.B: A source of light produced by spontaneous emission
options.C: A source of light produced by thermal radiation
options.D: A source of light produced by chemical reactions

questions.explanation: A laser is a source of light produced by stimulated emission; laser light is typically highly directional, coherent and narrow in wavelength range.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an important application of lasers?

options.A: Optical communication
options.B: Surgery

questions.explanation: Important applications of lasers include optical communication, surgery, cutting and welding, barcode scanners, range finding, spectroscopy, data storage and scientific research.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is sound?

options.A: A mechanical disturbance that propagates through a material medium as a wave and is perceived by the ear; sound cannot travel through a vacuum
options.B: An electromagnetic wave that can travel through a vacuum
options.C: A stream of particles that can travel through a vacuum
options.D: A type of radiation emitted by radioactive materials

questions.explanation: Sound is a mechanical disturbance that propagates through a material medium as a wave and is perceived by the ear; sound cannot travel through a vacuum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is sound produced?

options.A: By vibrating objects that set the surrounding medium into vibration
options.B: By static electric charges

questions.explanation: Sound is produced by vibrating objects that set the surrounding medium into vibration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How does sound propagate in air?

options.A: As longitudinal pressure waves consisting of compressions and rarefactions
options.B: As transverse waves consisting of crests and troughs

questions.explanation: Sound propagates in air as longitudinal pressure waves consisting of compressions and rarefactions.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a mechanical wave?

options.A: A wave that requires a material medium for propagation; examples include sound and water surface waves
options.B: A wave that can travel through a vacuum
options.C: A wave that consists of electric and magnetic fields
options.D: A wave that consists of particles

questions.explanation: A mechanical wave is a wave that requires a material medium for propagation; examples include sound and water surface waves.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a longitudinal wave?

options.A: A wave in which particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation; sound in air is longitudinal
options.B: A wave in which particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation
options.C: A wave that can travel through a vacuum
options.D: A wave that consists of electric and magnetic fields

questions.explanation: A longitudinal wave is a wave in which particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of wave propagation; sound in air is longitudinal.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a transverse wave?

options.A: A wave in which oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation; waves on a stretched string are a common example
options.B: A wave in which oscillations are parallel to the direction of propagation
options.C: A wave that requires no medium
options.D: A wave that consists of compressions and rarefactions

questions.explanation: A transverse wave is a wave in which oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of propagation; waves on a stretched string are a common example.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is wavelength?

options.A: The distance between successive points in the same phase, such as compression to compression; symbol λ, SI unit metre
options.B: The number of complete oscillations per second
options.D: The time taken for one complete oscillation

questions.explanation: Wavelength is the distance between successive points in the same phase, such as compression to compression; symbol λ, SI unit metre.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is frequency?

options.A: Number of complete oscillations or cycles per second; symbol f, SI unit hertz (Hz)
options.B: The distance between successive points in the same phase
options.D: The time taken for one complete oscillation

questions.explanation: Frequency is the number of complete oscillations or cycles per second; symbol f, SI unit hertz (Hz).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is amplitude?

options.A: Maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its equilibrium position; for sound, greater amplitude generally corresponds to greater intensity
options.B: The distance between successive points in the same phase
options.C: The number of complete oscillations per second
options.D: The time taken for one complete oscillation

questions.explanation: Amplitude is the maximum displacement of a vibrating particle from its equilibrium position; for sound, greater amplitude generally corresponds to greater intensity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is time period?

options.A: Time taken for one complete oscillation; T = 1/f, measured in seconds
options.B: The distance between successive points in the same phase
options.C: The number of complete oscillations per second

questions.explanation: Time period is the time taken for one complete oscillation; T = 1/f, measured in seconds.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is wave velocity?

options.A: Speed at which a wave disturbance travels; v = fλ
options.B: The distance between successive points in the same phase
options.C: The number of complete oscillations per second

questions.explanation: Wave velocity is the speed at which a wave disturbance travels; v = fλ.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What determines pitch?

options.A: Frequency: higher frequency is perceived as higher pitch
options.B: Amplitude: higher amplitude is perceived as higher pitch
options.C: Wavelength: longer wavelength is perceived as higher pitch
options.D: Speed: higher speed is perceived as higher pitch

questions.explanation: Pitch is determined by frequency: higher frequency is perceived as higher pitch.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What determines loudness?

options.A: Primarily sound intensity at the ear, which depends on wave amplitude and distance, as well as frequency and hearing sensitivity
options.B: Primarily frequency

questions.explanation: Loudness is primarily sound intensity at the ear, which depends on wave amplitude and distance, as well as frequency and hearing sensitivity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is sound intensity?

options.A: Sound power passing per unit area perpendicular to propagation; SI unit W/m²
options.B: The maximum displacement of a vibrating particle
options.C: The distance between successive points in the same phase
options.D: The number of complete oscillations per second

questions.explanation: Sound intensity is sound power passing per unit area perpendicular to propagation; SI unit W/m².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the normal human audible frequency range?

options.A: Approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), with variation by age and individual
options.B: Approximately 2 Hz to 2,000 Hz

questions.explanation: The normal human audible frequency range is approximately 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz), with variation by age and individual.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are infrasonic waves?

options.A: Sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz; examples include some earthquake and elephant communication signals
options.B: Sound waves with frequencies above 20 kHz
options.C: Sound waves with frequencies between 20 Hz and 20 kHz
options.D: Electromagnetic waves with frequencies below 20 Hz

questions.explanation: Infrasonic waves are sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz; examples include some earthquake and elephant communication signals.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are ultrasonic waves?

options.A: Sound waves with frequencies above 20 kHz; used in medical imaging, cleaning, flaw detection and SONAR
options.B: Sound waves with frequencies below 20 Hz
options.C: Sound waves with frequencies between 20 Hz and 20 kHz
options.D: Electromagnetic waves with frequencies above 20 kHz

questions.explanation: Ultrasonic waves are sound waves with frequencies above 20 kHz; used in medical imaging, cleaning, flaw detection and SONAR.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an echo?

options.A: A reflected sound heard separately from the original sound; in ordinary conditions, a time gap of about 0.1 s is needed for distinct perception
options.B: Persistence of sound in an enclosure due to repeated reflections
options.C: The bending of sound around obstacles
options.D: The change in frequency due to relative motion

questions.explanation: An echo is a reflected sound heard separately from the original sound; in ordinary conditions, a time gap of about 0.1 s is needed for distinct perception.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the approximate minimum distance for a distinct echo in air?

options.A: About 17 m from a large reflecting surface, assuming sound speed around 340 m/s and a 0.1 s persistence interval
options.B: About 34 m from a large reflecting surface
options.C: About 8.5 m from a large reflecting surface
options.D: About 170 m from a large reflecting surface

questions.explanation: The approximate minimum distance for a distinct echo in air is about 17 m from a large reflecting surface, assuming sound speed around 340 m/s and a 0.1 s persistence interval.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is reverberation?

options.A: Persistence of sound in an enclosure due to repeated reflections after the source stops; excessive reverberation reduces speech clarity
options.B: A reflected sound heard separately from the original sound
options.C: The bending of sound around obstacles
options.D: The change in frequency due to relative motion

questions.explanation: Reverberation is the persistence of sound in an enclosure due to repeated reflections after the source stops; excessive reverberation reduces speech clarity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is reverberation controlled in halls?

options.A: By using sound-absorbing materials such as acoustic tiles, curtains, carpets and upholstered seating, and by suitable hall design
options.B: By using sound-reflecting materials
options.C: By increasing the volume of the sound source
options.D: By removing all furniture from the hall

questions.explanation: Reverberation is controlled in halls by using sound-absorbing materials such as acoustic tiles, curtains, carpets and upholstered seating, and by suitable hall design.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is SONAR?

options.A: Sound Navigation And Ranging; it uses reflected underwater sound waves to detect objects and measure distance or depth
options.B: Sound Observation Navigation And Ranging
options.C: A system that uses electromagnetic waves to detect objects underwater
options.D: A system that uses light waves to detect objects underwater

questions.explanation: SONAR stands for Sound Navigation And Ranging; it uses reflected underwater sound waves to detect objects and measure distance or depth.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How is distance measured using echo?

options.A: Distance = (speed of sound × round-trip time)/2, because the sound travels to the object and back
options.B: Distance = speed of sound × round-trip time
options.D: Distance = speed of sound / round-trip time

questions.explanation: Distance is measured using echo as: distance = (speed of sound × round-trip time)/2, because the sound travels to the object and back.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the Doppler effect?

options.A: The apparent change in frequency (and wavelength) due to relative motion between a wave source and an observer
options.B: The bending of waves around obstacles
options.C: The persistence of sound in an enclosure
options.D: The change in direction of light when it passes between media

questions.explanation: The Doppler effect is the apparent change in frequency (and wavelength) due to relative motion between a wave source and an observer.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an application of ultrasound?

options.A: Medical ultrasonography
options.B: Echocardiography

questions.explanation: Applications of ultrasound include medical ultrasonography, echocardiography, kidney-stone fragmentation, industrial flaw detection, ultrasonic cleaning and distance measurement.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is noise pollution?

options.A: Unwanted or harmful sound that can disturb activities or damage health; prolonged exposure can cause hearing loss, sleep disturbance and stress
options.B: Sound with frequencies below 20 Hz
options.D: A reflected sound heard separately from the original sound

questions.explanation: Noise pollution is unwanted or harmful sound that can disturb activities or damage health; prolonged exposure can cause hearing loss, sleep disturbance and stress.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How can noise pollution be reduced?

options.A: Maintain vehicles and machinery, use silencers and sound barriers, enforce noise limits, avoid unnecessary horns and fireworks, and use hearing protection in high-noise workplaces
options.B: Increase the volume of sound sources
options.C: Remove all sound-absorbing materials from halls

questions.explanation: Noise pollution can be reduced by maintaining vehicles and machinery, using silencers and sound barriers, enforcing noise limits, avoiding unnecessary horns and fireworks, and using hearing protection in high-noise workplaces.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the basic structure of an atom?

options.A: An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons occupying quantum states around the nucleus
options.B: An atom has a large nucleus containing electrons
options.C: An atom has a nucleus containing only protons
options.D: An atom has a nucleus containing only neutrons

questions.explanation: An atom has a tiny, dense nucleus containing protons and neutrons, with electrons occupying quantum states around the nucleus.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relative charge of an electron?
questions.explanation: Electron: -1, proton: +1, neutron: 0, in units of the elementary charge.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relative charge of a proton?
questions.explanation: Electron: -1, proton: +1, neutron: 0, in units of the elementary charge.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the relative charge of a neutron?
questions.explanation: Electron: -1, proton: +1, neutron: 0, in units of the elementary charge.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who discovered the electron?

options.A: J. J. Thomson
options.B: Ernest Rutherford

questions.explanation: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron through cathode-ray experiments in 1897.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who discovered the atomic nucleus?

options.A: J. J. Thomson
options.B: Ernest Rutherford

questions.explanation: Ernest Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus from the gold-foil scattering experiment (published in 1911).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who is credited with identifying the proton?

options.A: J. J. Thomson
options.B: Ernest Rutherford

questions.explanation: Ernest Rutherford is credited with identifying the hydrogen nucleus as a fundamental nuclear particle (1917-1919).

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who discovered the neutron?

options.A: J. J. Thomson
options.B: Ernest Rutherford

questions.explanation: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an atomic number?

options.A: The number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the chemical element
options.B: The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus
options.C: The number of neutrons in the nucleus
options.D: The number of electrons in the outermost shell

questions.explanation: Atomic number is the number of protons in the nucleus; it identifies the chemical element.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a mass number?

options.A: The number of protons in the nucleus
options.B: The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus
options.C: The number of neutrons in the nucleus
options.D: The number of electrons in the outermost shell

questions.explanation: Mass number is the total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are isotopes?

options.A: Atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers
options.B: Atoms of different elements with the same mass number
options.C: Atoms with the same number of neutrons but different atomic numbers
options.D: Atoms with the same number of electrons but different atomic numbers

questions.explanation: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same atomic number but different numbers of neutrons and therefore different mass numbers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is radioactivity?

options.A: Spontaneous disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei with emission of ionising radiation
options.B: The splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei
options.C: The combining of light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
options.D: The emission of electrons from a material when light is incident on it

questions.explanation: Radioactivity is the spontaneous disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei with emission of ionising radiation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are alpha particles?

options.A: Helium-4 nuclei containing two protons and two neutrons; they have +2e charge, high ionising power and low penetration compared with beta and gamma radiation
options.B: High-speed electrons emitted in certain nuclear transformations
options.C: High-energy electromagnetic photons emitted by nuclear transitions

questions.explanation: Alpha particles are helium-4 nuclei containing two protons and two neutrons; they have +2e charge, high ionising power and low penetration compared with beta and gamma radiation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are beta particles?

options.A: Helium-4 nuclei containing two protons and two neutrons
options.B: High-speed electrons (β⁻) or positrons (β⁺) emitted in certain nuclear transformations; they have moderate penetration and are deflected by electric and magnetic fields
options.C: High-energy electromagnetic photons emitted by nuclear transitions

questions.explanation: Beta particles are high-speed electrons (β⁻) or positrons (β⁺) emitted in certain nuclear transformations; they have moderate penetration and are deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are gamma rays?

options.A: Helium-4 nuclei containing two protons and two neutrons
options.B: High-speed electrons emitted in certain nuclear transformations
options.C: High-energy electromagnetic photons emitted by nuclear transitions; they have no charge, very high penetration and are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields

questions.explanation: Gamma rays are high-energy electromagnetic photons emitted by nuclear transitions; they have no charge, very high penetration and are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do alpha, beta and gamma radiations compare in ionising power?

options.A: Alpha > Beta > Gamma
options.B: Gamma > Beta > Alpha

questions.explanation: Typical ionising power: alpha > beta > gamma; typical penetrating power: gamma > beta > alpha.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How do alpha, beta and gamma radiations compare in penetrating power?

options.A: Alpha > Beta > Gamma
options.B: Gamma > Beta > Alpha

questions.explanation: Typical penetrating power: gamma > beta > alpha. Shielding depends on energy and material; paper can stop many alpha particles, thin metal/plastic can reduce beta, and dense thick shielding attenuates gamma.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is nuclear fission?

options.A: Splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, usually releasing energy and neutrons; the neutrons may sustain a chain reaction
options.B: Combining light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus
options.C: Spontaneous disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei
options.D: Emission of electrons from a material when light is incident on it

questions.explanation: Nuclear fission is the splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei, usually releasing energy and neutrons; the neutrons may sustain a chain reaction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is nuclear fusion?

options.A: Splitting of a heavy nucleus into lighter nuclei
options.B: Combining light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy when the products have greater binding energy per nucleon; it powers the Sun and stars
options.C: Spontaneous disintegration of unstable atomic nuclei
options.D: Emission of electrons from a material when light is incident on it

questions.explanation: Nuclear fusion is combining light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy when the products have greater binding energy per nucleon; it powers the Sun and stars.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the main difference between fission and fusion?

options.A: Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei. Both can release nuclear energy
options.B: Fission joins light nuclei; fusion splits heavy nuclei
options.C: Fission releases energy; fusion does not
options.D: Fusion releases energy; fission does not

questions.explanation: The main difference is that fission splits heavy nuclei while fusion joins light nuclei. Both can release nuclear energy.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a nuclear chain reaction?

options.A: A sequence in which neutrons from one fission event cause further fissions; it may be controlled in a reactor
options.B: A sequence in which light nuclei combine to form heavier nuclei

questions.explanation: A nuclear chain reaction is a sequence in which neutrons from one fission event cause further fissions; it may be controlled in a reactor.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a nuclear reactor?

options.A: A facility in which a controlled nuclear fission chain reaction produces heat, commonly used to generate electricity
options.B: A facility in which an uncontrolled nuclear fission chain reaction occurs
options.C: A facility in which nuclear fusion powers the Sun
options.D: A facility that stores radioactive waste

questions.explanation: A nuclear reactor is a facility in which a controlled nuclear fission chain reaction produces heat, commonly used to generate electricity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are the main components of a nuclear reactor?

options.A: Fuel, moderator (in many reactor types), control rods, coolant, reactor vessel/core and shielding/containment
options.B: Fuel, moderator, control rods and coolant only

questions.explanation: The main components of a nuclear reactor include fuel, moderator (in many reactor types), control rods, coolant, reactor vessel/core and shielding/containment; designs vary.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of a moderator in a nuclear reactor?

options.A: In reactors that use one, it slows fast neutrons to energies that make further fission more likely; examples include ordinary water, heavy water and graphite
options.B: It absorbs neutrons to regulate or shut down the chain reaction
options.C: It removes heat from the reactor core
options.D: It shields the reactor from radiation

questions.explanation: In reactors that use a moderator, it slows fast neutrons to energies that make further fission more likely; examples include ordinary water, heavy water and graphite.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of control rods in a nuclear reactor?

options.A: They absorb neutrons to regulate or shut down the chain reaction; materials include boron, cadmium and hafnium
options.B: They slow fast neutrons to energies that make further fission more likely
options.C: They remove heat from the reactor core
options.D: They shield the reactor from radiation

questions.explanation: Control rods absorb neutrons to regulate or shut down the chain reaction; materials include boron, cadmium and hafnium.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of coolant in a nuclear reactor?

options.A: It removes heat from the reactor core and transfers it for useful purposes, often steam generation
options.B: It slows fast neutrons to energies that make further fission more likely
options.C: It absorbs neutrons to regulate or shut down the chain reaction
options.D: It shields the reactor from radiation

questions.explanation: Coolant removes heat from the reactor core and transfers it for useful purposes, often steam generation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is nuclear energy?

options.A: Energy associated with changes in atomic nuclei, including fission, fusion and radioactive decay
options.B: Energy associated with chemical reactions
options.C: Energy associated with the motion of electrons

questions.explanation: Nuclear energy is energy associated with changes in atomic nuclei, including fission, fusion and radioactive decay.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an application of atomic/nuclear energy?

options.A: Electricity generation
options.B: Medical diagnosis and cancer treatment

questions.explanation: Applications of atomic/nuclear energy include electricity generation, medical diagnosis and cancer treatment, industrial radiography, research, food irradiation and some space power systems.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What are X-rays?

options.A: High-energy electromagnetic radiation, commonly produced when fast electrons are decelerated or when inner-shell atomic electrons change energy levels
options.B: High-speed electrons emitted in certain nuclear transformations
options.C: Helium-4 nuclei containing two protons and two neutrons
options.D: High-energy electromagnetic photons emitted by nuclear transitions

questions.explanation: X-rays are high-energy electromagnetic radiation, commonly produced when fast electrons are decelerated or when inner-shell atomic electrons change energy levels.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who discovered X-rays?

options.A: J. J. Thomson
options.B: Ernest Rutherford

questions.explanation: Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen discovered X-rays in 1895.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an important application of X-rays?

options.A: Medical imaging
options.B: CT scanning

questions.explanation: Important applications of X-rays include medical imaging, CT scanning, security screening, crystallography and industrial inspection; exposure is controlled because X-rays are ionising.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the photoelectric effect?

options.A: Emission of electrons from a material when light of sufficiently high frequency is incident on it; below the threshold frequency, increasing intensity alone does not cause emission
options.B: Emission of light from a material when heated
options.C: Emission of X-rays when fast electrons are decelerated
options.D: Emission of alpha particles from unstable nuclei

questions.explanation: The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a material when light of sufficiently high frequency is incident on it; below the threshold frequency, increasing intensity alone does not cause emission.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Who explained the photoelectric effect using light quanta?

options.A: Albert Einstein
options.B: J. J. Thomson

questions.explanation: Albert Einstein explained the photoelectric effect using light quanta in 1905; the explanation supported the photon concept and earned him the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a photon?

options.A: A quantum of electromagnetic radiation; its energy is E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is frequency
options.B: A quantum of sound energy
options.C: A particle with mass and charge

questions.explanation: A photon is a quantum of electromagnetic radiation; its energy is E = hf, where h is Planck's constant and f is frequency.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a semiconductor?

options.A: A material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator and can be controlled by doping, temperature, light or electric fields; silicon and germanium are examples
options.B: A material that conducts electricity perfectly
options.C: A material that does not conduct electricity at all
options.D: A material that conducts electricity only at high temperatures

questions.explanation: A semiconductor is a material whose electrical conductivity lies between that of a conductor and an insulator and can be controlled by doping, temperature, light or electric fields; silicon and germanium are examples.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is doping in semiconductors?

options.A: Intentional addition of controlled impurities to change carrier concentration and electrical properties
options.B: Removal of impurities to change electrical properties
options.C: Heating a semiconductor to change its properties
options.D: Cooling a semiconductor to change its properties

questions.explanation: Doping in semiconductors is the intentional addition of controlled impurities to change carrier concentration and electrical properties.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an n-type semiconductor?

options.A: A semiconductor doped with donor impurities; electrons are the majority charge carriers
options.B: A semiconductor doped with acceptor impurities; holes are the majority charge carriers
options.D: A semiconductor that conducts only at high temperatures

questions.explanation: An n-type semiconductor is doped with donor impurities; electrons are the majority charge carriers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a p-type semiconductor?

options.A: A semiconductor doped with donor impurities; electrons are the majority charge carriers
options.B: A semiconductor doped with acceptor impurities; holes are the majority charge carriers
options.D: A semiconductor that conducts only at high temperatures

questions.explanation: A p-type semiconductor is doped with acceptor impurities; holes are the majority charge carriers.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a diode?

options.A: A two-terminal semiconductor device, commonly a p-n junction, that conducts readily in forward bias and blocks most current in reverse bias within its rating
options.B: A three-terminal semiconductor device used to amplify or switch electronic signals
options.C: A device that converts light energy directly into electrical energy
options.D: A device that emits light when forward biased

questions.explanation: A diode is a two-terminal semiconductor device, commonly a p-n junction, that conducts readily in forward bias and blocks most current in reverse bias within its rating.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a transistor?

options.A: A semiconductor device used to amplify or switch electronic signals; common types include bipolar junction transistors and field-effect transistors
options.B: A two-terminal semiconductor device that conducts in one direction
options.C: A device that converts light energy directly into electrical energy
options.D: A device that emits light when forward biased

questions.explanation: A transistor is a semiconductor device used to amplify or switch electronic signals; common types include bipolar junction transistors and field-effect transistors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is a solar cell?

options.A: A photovoltaic device that converts light energy directly into electrical energy using the photovoltaic effect, commonly in a semiconductor p-n junction
options.B: A device that converts electrical energy into light energy
options.C: A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy
options.D: A device that converts heat energy into electrical energy

questions.explanation: A solar cell is a photovoltaic device that converts light energy directly into electrical energy using the photovoltaic effect, commonly in a semiconductor p-n junction.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is an LED?

options.A: A light-emitting diode that emits light when forward biased as electrons and holes recombine; it is efficient and widely used in displays and lighting
options.B: A device that converts light energy directly into electrical energy
options.C: A device that amplifies electronic signals
options.D: A device that converts mechanical energy into electrical energy

questions.explanation: An LED (light-emitting diode) emits light when forward biased as electrons and holes recombine; it is efficient and widely used in displays and lighting.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the difference between an LED and an ordinary diode?

options.A: Both are semiconductor diodes; an LED is designed to emit useful light under forward bias, while an ordinary rectifier diode is primarily designed for current rectification
options.B: An LED is not a semiconductor device
options.C: An ordinary diode emits light under forward bias
options.D: An LED is designed for current rectification

questions.explanation: Both are semiconductor diodes; an LED is designed to emit useful light under forward bias, while an ordinary rectifier diode is primarily designed for current rectification.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is an important application of modern physics?

options.A: Nuclear power
options.B: Medical imaging and radiotherapy

questions.explanation: Important applications of modern physics include nuclear power, medical imaging and radiotherapy, semiconductor electronics, computers, lasers, fibre-optic communication, solar cells, atomic clocks and scientific instrumentation.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a correct distinction for exam purposes?

options.A: Mass is measured in kg and weight in N
options.B: Mass is measured in N and weight in kg
options.C: Heat is measured in K and temperature in J
options.D: Distance is a vector and displacement is a scalar

questions.explanation: Do not confuse mass (kg) with weight (N), or heat (J) with temperature (K or °C). Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are vectors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: At the highest point of vertical upward motion, what is true?

options.A: Instantaneous velocity is zero but acceleration due to gravity is still downward
options.B: Instantaneous velocity is maximum and acceleration is zero
options.C: Instantaneous velocity is zero and acceleration is zero
options.D: Instantaneous velocity is maximum and acceleration is downward

questions.explanation: At the highest point of vertical upward motion, instantaneous velocity is zero but acceleration due to gravity is still downward.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Action and reaction forces act on:

options.A: Different bodies; they do not cancel each other on one body
options.B: The same body; they cancel each other
options.C: The same body but in the same direction
options.D: Different bodies but in the same direction

questions.explanation: Action and reaction forces act on different bodies; they do not cancel each other on one body.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: An object in uniform circular motion has:

options.A: Constant speed but changing velocity and non-zero centripetal acceleration
options.B: Constant velocity and zero acceleration

questions.explanation: An object in uniform circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity and non-zero centripetal acceleration.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Work is zero when:

options.A: Force is perpendicular to displacement, even if a force acts
options.B: Force is parallel to displacement
options.C: Force is at an angle of 45° to displacement
options.D: Force and displacement are in the same direction

questions.explanation: Work is zero when force is perpendicular to displacement, even if a force acts.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following statements about relative density is correct?

options.A: Relative density has no unit; density has SI unit kg/m³
options.B: Relative density has SI unit kg/m³
options.C: Relative density has SI unit N/m³
options.D: Relative density has SI unit kg/m²

questions.explanation: Relative density has no unit. Density has SI unit kg/m³.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Pressure in a liquid at rest depends on:

options.A: Depth and density, not on the container's shape
options.B: The container's shape only
options.D: The volume of the liquid only

questions.explanation: Pressure in a liquid at rest depends on depth and density, not on the container's shape.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Water has maximum density at:

options.A: 4 °C at standard atmospheric pressure
options.B: 0 °C at standard atmospheric pressure

questions.explanation: Water has maximum density near 4 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following statements about evaporation and boiling is correct?

options.A: Evaporation can occur at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling condition
options.B: Evaporation occurs only at the boiling point; boiling can occur at any temperature
options.C: Both evaporation and boiling occur only at the boiling point
options.D: Both evaporation and boiling can occur at any temperature

questions.explanation: Evaporation can occur at any temperature; boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling condition.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which mode of heat transfer can travel through a vacuum?

options.A: Radiation
options.B: Conduction

questions.explanation: Radiation can travel through vacuum; conduction and convection require matter.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: An ideal transformer requires:

options.A: Changing magnetic flux and therefore works with AC, not steady DC
options.B: Steady magnetic flux and therefore works with DC
options.C: Constant current and therefore works with DC

questions.explanation: An ideal transformer requires changing magnetic flux and therefore works with AC, not steady DC.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Household appliances are connected in:

options.A: Parallel, not series
options.B: Series, not parallel
options.C: A combination of series and parallel only

questions.explanation: Household appliances are connected in parallel, not series.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the function of a fuse and an MCB?

options.A: They protect against excessive current; earthing is a protective measure against electric shock
options.B: They protect against electric shock; earthing protects against excessive current
options.C: They increase the current in a circuit

questions.explanation: Fuse and MCB protect against excessive current; earthing is a protective measure against electric shock.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What type of image does a convex mirror always form?

options.A: Virtual, erect, diminished
options.B: Real, inverted, magnified

questions.explanation: Convex mirrors always give virtual, erect, diminished images; concave mirrors can give real or virtual images.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Myopia is corrected by a:

options.A: Concave lens
options.B: Convex lens

questions.explanation: Myopia is corrected by a concave lens; hypermetropia by a convex lens.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Hypermetropia is corrected by a:

options.A: Concave lens
options.B: Convex lens

questions.explanation: Hypermetropia is corrected by a convex lens; myopia by a concave lens.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which colour of light has a longer wavelength in the visible spectrum?

options.A: Red
options.B: Violet

questions.explanation: Red light has a longer wavelength than violet light in the visible spectrum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following statements about sound and light is correct?

options.A: Sound needs a medium; light can travel through vacuum
options.B: Light needs a medium; sound can travel through vacuum
options.C: Both sound and light need a medium
options.D: Neither sound nor light needs a medium

questions.explanation: Sound needs a medium; light can travel through vacuum.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Pitch depends mainly on:

options.A: Frequency
options.B: Intensity at the ear

questions.explanation: Pitch depends mainly on frequency; loudness depends mainly on intensity at the ear.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Loudness depends mainly on:

options.A: Frequency
options.B: Intensity at the ear

questions.explanation: Loudness depends mainly on intensity at the ear; pitch depends mainly on frequency.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following statements about alpha and gamma radiation is correct?

options.A: Alpha radiation is highly ionising but weakly penetrating; gamma radiation is highly penetrating
options.B: Alpha radiation is weakly ionising but highly penetrating; gamma radiation is weakly penetrating
options.C: Both alpha and gamma radiation are highly ionising and highly penetrating
options.D: Both alpha and gamma radiation are weakly ionising and weakly penetrating

questions.explanation: Alpha radiation is highly ionising but weakly penetrating; gamma radiation is highly penetrating.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following statements about fission and fusion is correct?

options.A: Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei
options.B: Fission joins light nuclei; fusion splits heavy nuclei
options.C: Both fission and fusion split heavy nuclei
options.D: Both fission and fusion join light nuclei

questions.explanation: Fission splits heavy nuclei; fusion joins light nuclei.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A solar cell converts:

options.A: Light directly into electricity
options.B: Electricity into light

questions.explanation: A solar cell converts light directly into electricity; an LED converts electrical energy into light.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: An LED converts:

options.A: Light directly into electricity
options.B: Electrical energy into light

questions.explanation: An LED converts electrical energy into light; a solar cell converts light directly into electricity.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following instruments is used to measure internal and external dimensions and depth?

options.A: Vernier callipers
options.B: Screw gauge

questions.explanation: Vernier callipers measure internal/external dimensions and depth, while a screw gauge measures very small thickness or diameter.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a scalar quantity?

options.A: Distance
options.B: Displacement

questions.explanation: Distance is a scalar quantity; displacement, velocity and force are vectors.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Which of the following is a vector quantity?

options.A: Speed
options.B: Mass

questions.explanation: Displacement is a vector quantity; speed, mass and time are scalars.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: If a body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration a for time t, what is its displacement?

options.A: s = ½at²
options.B: s = at²

questions.explanation: Using s = ut + ½at² with u = 0, s = ½at².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A car accelerates from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 5 s. What is its acceleration?

options.A: 4 m/s²
options.B: 5 m/s²

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A body moving with uniform velocity has:

options.A: Zero acceleration
options.B: Constant acceleration

questions.explanation: Uniform velocity means velocity is constant, so acceleration is zero.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the SI unit of momentum?

options.A: kg m/s
options.B: kg m/s²

questions.explanation: The SI unit of momentum is kg m/s, which is also equivalent to N s.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the formula for centripetal force?

options.A: F = mv²/r
options.B: F = mv/r

questions.explanation: Centripetal force is given by F = mv²/r, directed towards the centre of the circular path.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the formula for weight?

options.A: W = mg
options.B: W = m/g

questions.explanation: Weight is the gravitational force on an object: W = mg.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the formula for kinetic energy?

options.A: KE = ½mv²
options.B: KE = mv²

questions.explanation: Kinetic energy is given by KE = ½mv².

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the formula for gravitational potential energy near Earth's surface?

options.A: PE = ½mv²
options.B: PE = mgh

questions.explanation: Near Earth's surface, gravitational potential energy relative to a chosen level is PE = mgh.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A body of mass 2 kg moves with velocity 3 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

options.A: 6 J
options.B: 9 J

questions.explanation: KE = ½mv² = ½ × 2 × 3² = 9 J.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A machine does 1000 J of work in 10 s. What is its power?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A body of volume 0.02 m³ is immersed in water of density 1000 kg/m³. What is the buoyant force? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Buoyant force = weight of displaced water = ρVg = 1000 × 0.02 × 10 = 200 N.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: What is the gauge pressure at a depth of 5 m in water? (ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s²)

options.B: 500 Pa

questions.explanation: Gauge pressure p = ρgh = 1000 × 10 × 5 = 50,000 Pa.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 2 kg of a substance by 10 K if its specific heat capacity is 500 J/kgK?

questions.question: A current of 2 A flows through a resistor of 5 Ω. What is the potential difference across it?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in series. What is the equivalent resistance?
questions.explanation: In series, R = R₁ + R₂ = 4 + 6 = 10 Ω.

questions.question: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: An electric bulb of power 100 W is used for 5 hours. How much energy does it consume?

options.A: 0.5 kWh
options.B: 5 kWh

questions.explanation: Energy = power × time = 0.1 kW × 5 h = 0.5 kWh.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A current of 3 A flows through a resistor of 4 Ω for 10 s. What is the heat produced?

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: An object is placed 20 cm from a plane mirror. What is the distance between the object and its image?

options.A: 20 cm
options.B: 40 cm

questions.explanation: The image is formed 20 cm behind the mirror, so the distance between the object and its image is 20 + 20 = 40 cm.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: The power of a lens is -2 D. What is its focal length?
questions.explanation: P = 1/f, so f = 1/P = 1/(-2) = -0.5 m. The negative sign indicates a concave lens.

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A wave has frequency 50 Hz and wavelength 4 m. What is its velocity?

options.B: 54 m/s

questions.subject: General Science
questions.question: A sound wave travels to a reflecting surface and back in 0.4 s. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, what is the distance to the surface?
questions.explanation: Distance = (speed × round-trip time)/2 = (340 × 0.4)/2 = 68 m.
